demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Mr. Khan keeps his small apartment meticulously ordered. His late wife’s photo is dusted daily, his shoes are aligned by the door, and the single framed picture on the wall—a younger, uniformed version of himself standing proudly on the deck of a cutter—is perfectly level. He spent forty years in the Coast Guard, a source of immense pride he can barely speak of now. He presents as a quiet, dignified man, his hands resting in his lap, but a persistent tremor in his right thumb betrays a deep and abiding unease.

Over our sessions, a picture has emerged of a life defined by duty, control, and one catastrophic moment when both failed him. He was 32 years old, a Petty Officer First Class, considered one of the most capable men on his ship. He speaks of that time with a detached clarity, as if describing another man. He was strong, respected, and unflappable, even in the teeth of a gale.

The night it happened was a maelstrom of freezing rain and violent waves off the coast. A fishing trawler had lost power and was being battered against a reef. The rescue was treacherous. Mr. Khan was operating the winch, his hands sure and steady as he lowered the rescue basket toward the floundering vessel. He remembers the salty spray freezing on his face, the shriek of wind and metal, the focused calm he felt as he maneuvered the basket through the chaos.

And then, a rogue wave, larger than the rest, slammed into the cutter. The ship lurched violently, and the winch cable, under immense tension, jumped its guide. For a split second, he lost control. The heavy basket swung like a pendulum, crashing into the trawler's deck where a young crewman, barely a man, was waiting to be lifted. Mr. Khan describes the image that is seared into his mind: the boy’s face, white in the floodlights, turning toward the impact an instant before it struck. He remembers the sickening crunch, a sound that was somehow louder than the storm itself.

An inquiry cleared him of any wrongdoing. It was deemed a tragic accident, an act of God. But for Mr. Khan, the verdict was meaningless. It was his hand on the controls. He had been entrusted with saving lives, and instead, he had grievously wounded someone. The young man survived, but with permanent, life-altering injuries. Mr. Khan never met him, never knew his name, which he says is somehow worse. The man is just a ghost, a face in a floodlight.

For decades, he buried the memory. He threw himself into his work, becoming even more exacting, more procedural. He raised a family with his wife, Safia, who he describes as his anchor. She seemed to understand there was a locked room inside him and never tried to force the door. But she was the buffer between him and the silence.

Two years ago, Safia passed away. The silence she held at bay flooded his life. Now, the storm is no longer a distant memory; it is a constant, intrusive presence. The clank of the radiator pipes in his apartment becomes the sound of the rescue basket striking steel. A car backfiring on the street sends a jolt of adrenaline through him that leaves him trembling. He spends hours staring out the window, his mind replaying the lurch of the deck, the slack in the cable, the boy’s face. Sleep offers little escape, often bringing him back to that slick, tilting deck. He no longer drives and has stopped visiting his children, ashamed of the irritable, anxious man he has become and unable to explain the source of a sorrow that is nearly fifty years old. He simply tells them he is tired. The uniform in the photograph on his wall seems to mock him now, a reminder of a man he no longer recognizes as himself.
